beats.intro: Lesson eighteen. [[sub]]Dual reporting at work, and the organization that runs on more than one plane.
beats.controller: A hybrid organization must get the functional groups' resources to where the mission units need them. Take a division's controller. [[ctrl]]He works inside the business division. [[fin]]But his methods, practices and standards come from finance. [[gm]]The general manager gives him mission priorities: specific business problems to work on. [[train]]The finance manager sees that he is trained, and supervises his technical performance, [[career]]and looks after his career in finance. Do well, and he may become controller of a bigger division.
beats.ads: Now advertising. Should each division run its own, or one corporate group? [[div]]Each division knows its own strategy best, so it knows its message and its audience. [[corp]]But several divisions' products often serve one market, and together are a fuller answer for the customer. Their stories should be coordinated. [[image]]And ads sell the whole company, so the image should be consistent. [[agency]]At the very least, no division should hire its own agency.
beats.adfix: The answer, again, is dual reporting. [[msg]]Division marketing managers control most of their own messages. [[council]]A body of their peers, perhaps chaired by the corporate merchandising manager, gives functional supervision. [[jobs]]It picks the agency, sets the graphic image, defines how divisions work with the agency, and buys space in volume, which cuts cost. [[patience]]It taxes everyone's patience, since they must understand their peers' needs. But there is no real alternative.
beats.univ: Every kind of organization ends up this way. Grove quotes a Wall Street Journal story about Ohio University, with his own notes added. [[admin]]Decisions were shared between the administration, the functional side, [[fac]]and the faculty, the mission side. [[council]]A planning council of peers from both was formed to share out scarce money during severe budget cuts. [[inst]]One member said, we are being educated to think institutionally. [[doze]]She represented student affairs, yet she made a big pitch for a new bulldozer.
beats.nobusy: So the hybrid form is the price of being part of something large. [[not]]It is no excuse for busywork. [[cut]]Slash needless bureaucracy, simplify the work, and test every coordination requirement against common sense. [[escape]]But don't expect to escape complexity by redrawing reporting lines. The hybrid organization is a basic fact of organizational life.
beats.planes: There is a subtler kind of dual reporting. Remember the process engineer from lesson twelve? [[op]]In her plant, she reports to a supervising engineer, and through him to the plant's engineering manager. That is eighty percent of her time. [[coord]]But once a month she meets her counterparts from the other plants, to solve problems with the same process and standardize procedures. [[chair]]The group's chairman supervises her work there. [[emc]]And such groups answer to the Engineering Managers Council, the engineering managers of every plant. [[two]]So her name is on two organization charts.
beats.church: Her two jobs won't fit on one chart, so think of the group as a different plane. [[church]]That sounds complicated, but it isn't. If she belonged to a church, she would be a member of it as well as of the company. [[pastor]]Her supervisor there would be the local pastor, part of the church's own hierarchy. [[clear]]Nobody would confuse the two.
beats.lever: And it multiplies her leverage. [[one]]In her main job, her know-how shapes one plant. [[all]]Through the group, it shapes every plant. [[know]]Coordinating groups let managers, especially know-how managers, increase their leverage.
beats.more: Planes are part of everyday life. [[plan]]People mostly do operating work, but they also plan, and planning bodies sit on a plane of their own. [[three]]If you can work in two planes, you can work in three: she could also join a task force that needs her expertise. [[like]]It's like working at the company, belonging to a church, and advising the town's parks department. [[time]]The roles don't conflict, but they all compete for her time.
beats.reverse: A boss in one plane may report to someone in another. [[pres]]Grove was president of Intel. [[group]]But in a strategic planning group, he reported to its chairman, a division controller. [[army]]Like the Army Reserve: on weekend exercises, the controller would be his commanding officer, [[ranch]]even though back at the operating ranch, Grove was his boss, or his boss's boss.
beats.soldier: Why is that useful? [[only]]Otherwise Grove could join only the groups he ran. [[time]]He didn't have that kind of time, [[qual]]and often he was not the most qualified to lead. [[foot]]So he could serve as a foot soldier, not a general, when that was right. [[flex]]That gives the organization flexibility.
beats.temp: Many of these groups are temporary. [[tf]]Task forces are formed for a purpose. [[inf]]Others are informal: a few people solving one problem. Both stop when it is solved. [[fast]]The faster things change, the more we rely on such short-lived teams. [[formal]]In electronics, Grove says, the formal organization can't change fast enough to keep up. [[need]]These teams need dual or multiple reporting, and decisions by peers. [[culture]]And they all depend on cultural values as a way of control. That is the next lesson.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]The mission side sets priorities; the function sets standards and careers. [[w2]]A council of peers keeps one image; divisions keep their messages. [[w3]]Cut busywork, but you can't reorganize complexity away. [[w4]]One person can work on several planes, for more leverage. [[w5]]Rank can reverse between planes, and change runs on temporary teams. Now the lesson practice.
beats.final1: Lesson practice. Five situations from a manager's week.
beats.finish: Well done. That is the end of lesson eighteen, and of Grove's chapter on dual reporting.
